justification_text:
This probabilistic forecast reflects my best estimate of how the underlying value or variable of interest might change over the next day, week, and month. For the point estimates at each horizon, they are based on the observable trend over time and any structural patterns or underlying factors that are likely to persist in the short term. For example, my 1-day and 1-week forecasts of 180.7 and 181.5, respectively, suggest that I anticipate a modest and steady increase in the variable over these shorter horizons. This could indicate underlying momentum or stability in the system. By the 1-month horizon (183.0), the point estimate reflects expectations of gradual growth continuing, assuming no major shocks or disruptions to the baseline trends.

The widths of the confidence intervals are driven by both the timeframe and the degree of uncertainty I associate with each horizon. In the short term, within one day, I assume limited variability because most systems tend to exhibit less dramatic shifts over a very short period, and thus the confidence interval is relatively tight (179.1 to 182.3). By the 1-week and 1-month horizons, however, the uncertainty compounds as more variables come into play, such as external shocks, random fluctuations, or shifts that accumulate over time. This growth in uncertainty widens the confidence intervals, ranging from 176.5 to 186.5 at one week and 173.0 to 193.0 by one month.

There are specific risks or events that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. For example, unexpected shocks such as major policy changes, market crashes, or disruptive geopolitical events could cause deviations far greater than anticipated. Similarly, the presence of low-probability, high-impact events—sometimes referred to as "Black Swan" events—could produce outcomes that fall well outside even the 90% confidence intervals. Lastly, if there is underlying instability in the system or if I underestimated the volatility of the variable, actual outcomes could also deviate from these projections. These risks underscore the probabilistic nature of forecasting, where uncertainty can never be entirely captured but is instead framed as best as possible with the available information.
